headline: Arabic language models have an industrial use case hiding in the document room
deck: Standards, permits, method statements, inspection reports and handover files are the largest unstructured text estate in Gulf industry.
excerpt: Sovereign artificial intelligence and Arabic language models are among the categories vendors will show at the Global AI Summit. The industrial application is unglamorous: the enormous volume of bilingual technical documentation that Gulf projects generate and rarely use again.
content:
Vendors at the Global AI Summit in Riyadh this week will show sovereign artificial intelligence, Arabic language models, computer vision and industry solutions for regulated sectors. The Arabic language work has an industrial application that is rarely discussed and is probably the largest one available.

Every industrial project in the Gulf generates an enormous estate of technical documentation. Standards and codes, permits and approvals, method statements, risk assessments, inspection and test plans, non-conformance reports, material certificates, commissioning records, as-built drawings and operation and maintenance manuals. On a large project it runs to hundreds of thousands of documents.

Most of it is written once, used during the phase it belongs to, filed at handover and never read again. The information it contains — what was installed, to what standard, tested how, with what deviations — is precisely what an operator needs decades later when deciding whether a vessel can run to the next turnaround or which valve was substituted during construction.

The retrieval problem is severe and it is bilingual. Regulatory material, permits and correspondence in the Gulf are frequently in Arabic; international standards, vendor documentation and engineering drawings are usually in English; and the same asset is described in both across different documents. A conventional search finds neither reliably.

That is a language model problem of exactly the kind these systems handle well: retrieval across a large corpus, in two languages, where the question is asked in one and the answer is written in the other.

The reason it matters industrially is that the alternative is a person. Assembling the documentary history of a single item of equipment before a turnaround decision is currently days of engineering time, and it is done selectively because it cannot be done for everything. The result is that integrity decisions are routinely made on a partial record, and the missing part is usually in a filing system rather than genuinely absent.

The caution is the familiar one. These systems are useful when they cite the document rather than summarise it, because a summary that is subtly wrong about a material certificate is worse than no summary. In a regulated environment the output has to be traceable to a source a competent person can check, which constrains how the technology is deployed rather than whether it is. Retrieval with citation is a narrower product than the assistants being demonstrated, and it is the one an operator can actually put into a permit-to-work process.

The sovereign dimension follows from the same requirement. Project documentation contains commercially sensitive and often security-sensitive information about critical infrastructure, and operators are unlikely to send it to a model hosted elsewhere. That is an argument for domestic capacity that stands on its own, independent of any national ambition.

The summit runs at the King Abdulaziz International Conference Centre from 15 to 17 September.
